## Brand Photography Brief: What to Give Your Creative Agency

A strong brand photography brief for an agency should explain what you sell, who the images are for, where they will be used, and what the agency must deliver. It should give enough direction to protect your brand without prescribing every pose, prop or camera angle before the creative work begins.

For an Indian small business, D2C brand, school, clinic, NGO or agency, the brief is also a planning document. It helps the creative team estimate the shoot, identify people and products required, plan locations, check permissions, and create photographs that work across Instagram, websites, marketplaces, brochures and advertisements.

## Why a Brand Photography Brief Matters

Many photography projects begin with a short message such as “We need new photos for social media.” That sounds clear, but it leaves important decisions unanswered.

The agency still needs to understand:

- Which products, services or people need to be photographed
- Whether the images are for a launch, an evergreen content library or a campaign
- Who will approve the work
- What visual style is appropriate
- Which platforms and image sizes are required
- Whether models, customers, children or staff will appear
- What budget and schedule constraints apply
- Whether the final images need editing, retouching or design adaptations

Without this information, the agency may plan a shoot that looks attractive but does not solve your actual communication problem. You may receive polished images that do not fit your website banner, social media templates, product listings or paid advertisements.

A brief gives both sides a common reference point. It reduces assumptions before the shoot and makes it easier to discuss changes when the first concepts are presented.

It does not need to be a formal document prepared by a large marketing department. A well-organised Google Doc or PDF of a few pages is usually enough, provided it answers the practical questions.

### The brief is not a mood board alone

A mood board can show colours, lighting and visual references. It cannot replace the business information the agency needs.

For example, three reference images may all use soft daylight, but one may be a product catalogue image, another a lifestyle photograph and the third a social media campaign image with empty space for text. The production requirements are different.

Use visual references alongside written direction. Explain what you like about each reference and what you do not want copied.

## Start With the Business Objective

The first section of your brief should explain why the photography is being commissioned. This helps the agency make decisions that support a business outcome rather than producing disconnected images.

Possible objectives include:

- Introducing a new D2C product range
- Replacing inconsistent images on an ecommerce website
- Building a six-month social media content library
- Showing the people behind a professional service
- Making a school or clinic appear more approachable and trustworthy
- Documenting an NGO’s programmes for donor communication
- Creating images for a seasonal campaign
- Supporting a website redesign
- Improving packaging, catalogue or marketplace listings
- Giving a creative agency reusable assets for future campaigns

Be specific about the business situation. Instead of writing “We want premium photos,” write:

> We are launching a small-batch skincare range and need product and lifestyle images for our website, Instagram, online marketplaces and retailer presentations. The photographs should feel clean, credible and warm, while showing how the products fit into a daily routine.

This gives the agency useful information about the audience, products, channels and tone.

### Identify the primary audience

Describe the people expected to see and act on the images. Include relevant context such as:

- Age range, if relevant
- City or region
- Language preferences
- Buying motivation
- Main concern or objection
- Whether they are consumers, donors, parents, students, patients or business buyers
- Whether the decision-maker and end user are different

An education brand may be speaking to parents while showing children and classrooms. A clinic may need to reassure patients without making medical claims. An NGO may be speaking to donors, volunteers and community members, each requiring a different visual approach.

### Define the intended action

Tell the agency what the audience should do after seeing the images. The action could be:

- Visit a website
- Enquire on WhatsApp
- Purchase a product
- Book an appointment
- Register for a course
- Donate
- Attend an event
- Contact a sales team
- Download a brochure

The photography will be planned differently if the images must support a direct sale compared with a general brand-awareness campaign.

## Explain Your Brand and Visual Direction

Your agency should not have to guess how your brand wants to be perceived. Include a short description of the brand personality and the qualities the images should communicate.

Useful descriptive words might include:

- Practical
- Friendly
- Modern
- Rooted in local culture
- Expert
- Accessible
- Premium but not formal
- Playful
- Minimal
- Community-focused
- Natural
- Energetic
- Trustworthy

Avoid listing too many contradictory adjectives. “Luxury, affordable, youthful, traditional, bold, understated and playful” does not give a clear direction. Select the qualities that matter most for this particular project.

### Share existing brand materials

Attach or link to:

- Logo files
- Brand guidelines
- Colour palette
- Font details
- Packaging artwork
- Website
- Social media pages
- Existing advertisements
- Previous photography
- Relevant illustrations or icons

If the business does not have formal brand guidelines, say so. The agency can then help establish a practical visual system during the project.

Also point out elements that must remain consistent. These might include a particular packaging colour, a uniform, a clinic interior, regional craft techniques or a founder’s appearance.

### State what to avoid

Negative direction is as useful as positive direction. Mention if you do not want:

- Heavy filters
- Artificial-looking skin retouching
- Stock-photo-style poses
- Cluttered backgrounds
- Excessive luxury cues
- Dark or dramatic lighting
- Religious or cultural symbols used casually
- Images that look too Western for your Indian customer base
- Generic office scenes
- Overly staged family interactions
- Visible competitor products
- Unapproved medical, environmental or social claims

This is especially important when the brand operates in a sensitive category. A healthcare provider, NGO or education institution should review whether images could create an inaccurate impression or expose people without proper consent.

## List the Exact Photography Requirements

The phrase “brand photography” may include several different types of work. Break the requirement into categories so the agency can plan properly.

### Product photography

Product photography may include:

- Plain-background pack shots
- Multiple angles
- Product groups or bundles
- Close-up details
- Scale references
- Packaging and labelling
- Products in use
- Product images with hands or people
- Flat lays
- Lifestyle settings
- Images with space for promotional text

If the images will be used on an ecommerce marketplace, check that platform’s current image rules before the shoot. Requirements may differ for background colour, product visibility, text, logos, props and image dimensions.

Also explain whether every variant needs to be photographed. A food or cosmetics brand may have several sizes, flavours, fragrances or shades. The agency needs the complete product list before planning.

### People and team photography

For founder, staff or team photographs, clarify whether you need:

- Individual portraits
- Group photographs
- Informal working images
- Customer-service interactions
- Behind-the-scenes images
- Professional headshots
- Images for speaker profiles
- Recruitment and employer-branding content

List the names and roles of people expected to participate. Check their availability in advance. If a founder or medical professional must be present, their schedule may affect the entire shoot.

For schools, NGOs and community projects, confirm whether children or vulnerable individuals may appear. Written consent and responsible handling of images should be planned before the camera is used.

### Location and service photography

Service businesses often need images that show an experience rather than a physical product. Examples include:

- A clinic reception and consultation environment
- A school classroom or activity
- A salon or studio session
- A consulting team working with a client
- An NGO field programme
- A restaurant kitchen or dining experience
- A manufacturing or workshop process

List the locations, access restrictions and activities that can realistically be photographed. A working clinic may need patient privacy protections. A school may need photography outside teaching hours. A factory may require safety equipment and permission from management.

### Social media content

If the main use is social media, do not request only “Instagram photos.” Explain the content formats required.

You may need:

- Portrait-oriented images for Reels and Stories
- Square images for feed posts
- Wide images for website banners
- Cropped details for carousel posts
- Images with empty areas for text overlays
- Short vertical videos or motion clips
- Repeated compositions that allow a consistent feed style

Ask the agency to recommend the necessary framing and file variations. A single photograph may not work equally well as a profile banner, a product listing and a vertical Story.

## Describe the Deliverables Clearly

A photography brief should define what you expect to receive after the shoot. Avoid relying only on the phrase “edited high-resolution images.”

Clarify:

- Approximate number of final photographs
- Number of products or setups
- Number of locations
- Whether images will be delivered in colour, black and white or both
- File format, such as JPEG, PNG or TIFF where relevant
- Resolution or intended usage
- Web-ready and high-resolution versions
- Cropped versions for social media
- Whether raw files are included
- Whether colour correction and retouching are included
- Whether background removal is required
- Whether text or graphic design is included
- Delivery method, such as a shared drive
- Naming and folder structure
- Expected review and revision process

The final image count should be discussed realistically. A shoot may produce many exposures, but that does not mean every exposure should be delivered. More files can create storage and selection problems for a small team.

### Separate photography from design

Photography, graphic design, video editing and social media content production are related but different services.

If you need designed Instagram posts, ask whether the agency is delivering:

1. The raw photographic asset
2. A retouched image
3. A social media crop
4. A complete designed post with copy and branding
5. A caption, carousel or Reel edit

Write the requirement separately for each item. This avoids confusion when a team delivers photographs but not finished social media creatives.

### Plan for future use

Ask how the files will be organised so your business can use them later. Useful file labels might include the product name, model or subject, location, date and orientation.

Keep a record of:

- Which people have signed consent forms
- Which products appear in each photograph
- Which images have usage restrictions
- Where the original files are stored
- Who owns the final assets
- Whether third-party fonts, music or props create additional rights issues

This record becomes valuable when you revisit the images months later.

## Include Logistics, Budget Inputs and Responsibilities

Good agency planning depends on operational details. Add a section that explains what your organisation will provide and what the agency must arrange.

### Your responsibilities may include

- Supplying clean and complete products
- Confirming product claims and labels
- Providing brand assets
- Arranging access to premises
- Identifying available staff or models
- Getting internal approvals
- Providing props or uniforms
- Arranging customer or participant consent
- Making decision-makers available
- Providing food, transport or accommodation where agreed
- Reviewing initial concepts on time

### The agency may need to arrange

- Photographer and assistants
- Studio or location
- Lighting and camera equipment
- Styling and set design
- Professional models
- Hair and makeup
- Props and surfaces
- Art direction
- Retouching
- Production management
- Travel and logistics
- Backup equipment

Do not assume these items are included. Ask for them to be listed separately in the proposal.

### Cost factors to discuss

Market costs vary significantly based on the photographer, location, number of products, production team, styling requirements, model licensing, post-production and usage rights. A small tabletop product shoot is planned differently from a multi-location campaign with professional models.

Ask the agency to identify:

- Creative and pre-production fee
- Photographer fee
- Studio or location costs
- Models and usage fees
- Styling and props
- Equipment
- Travel and accommodation
- Production assistants
- Editing and retouching
- Video or motion requirements
- GST
- Cancellation or rescheduling terms
- Additional revision charges
- Overtime or extra deliverables

Do not compare proposals only by the number of photographs. A lower quote may exclude styling, retouching, usage rights or social media adaptations that you later need.

## Cover Usage Rights, Consent and Compliance

Photography contracts should clearly address who may use the images, where they may be used and for how long.

Discuss whether the business can use the final images on:

- Its website
- Organic social media
- Paid advertising
- Ecommerce marketplaces
- Packaging
- Printed brochures
- Outdoor advertising
- Press coverage
- Investor or donor presentations
- Internal documents
- Partner or distributor channels

Model usage is particularly important. A model may agree to appear in a shoot, but the permitted use, duration, territory and paid advertising rights should be recorded. The same applies to photographers, illustrators, locations and stock elements.

### Consent for people in photographs

Obtain appropriate written consent from identifiable adults. Consent should explain the intended use in language the person understands.

For children, obtain consent from a parent or legal guardian and follow the institution’s safeguarding process. For NGO programmes or sensitive health and community settings, consider whether showing a person is genuinely necessary. A signed form alone does not remove the responsibility to protect dignity and privacy.

Do not publish identifiable patient information in a clinic photograph. Check screens, files, registers, name tags and whiteboards for personal data before shooting.

India’s Digital Personal Data Protection framework may be relevant when photographs are associated with identifiable individuals and used as personal data. Your organisation should take appropriate legal advice for its situation, especially for minors, patients, employees and beneficiaries.

### Ownership and portfolio use

Ask who owns the commissioned images after payment and what rights the agency retains. Some agencies may want to display the work on their website or social media. This is usually a separate consideration from your right to use the images.

If a campaign is confidential or has not launched, specify when the agency may publish behind-the-scenes content or final photographs.

## Use a Comparison Table Before Approving the Brief

A simple planning table can help connect each requirement to its purpose and production needs.

| Requirement | Intended use | Format or framing | People/products needed | Important notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Founder portrait | Website, LinkedIn, press | Vertical and horizontal | Founder, office or neutral setting | Leave space for text in one version |
| Product pack shot | Website and marketplace | Front-facing, clean background | All product variants | Confirm platform image rules |
| Product in use | Instagram and website | Portrait and square crops | Product, model, props | Show realistic Indian usage |
| Team interaction | About page and social media | Wide and portrait options | Named staff members | Avoid visible confidential information |
| Programme activity | NGO reports and social media | Documentary-style images | Participants with consent | Protect dignity and privacy |
| Clinic environment | Website and local listings | Wide and vertical | Staff, approved setting | No patient data in frame |

The table does not replace creative direction. It makes the scope visible and gives the agency a practical starting point.

## Build a Useful Reference Pack

Send your agency a reference pack rather than a random collection of saved images. Organise the references by purpose.

You could create sections for:

- Lighting
- Backgrounds and surfaces
- Product arrangement
- Human expressions
- Clothing
- Composition
- Colour treatment
- Degree of retouching
- Social media layout
- Images you want to avoid

For every important reference, add one sentence explaining what it shows. For example:

> We like the soft side lighting and the amount of empty space, but we do not want the dark brown colour palette.

Or:

> We like the candid interaction between the staff members. Please keep the body language natural rather than using formal office poses.

Include examples from your own industry, but do not limit the agency to competitor images. A school may find useful lighting ideas in a hospitality shoot, while a food brand may learn composition from an editorial photograph.

### Consider regional and cultural context

A visual direction that looks attractive online may not feel credible to your customers. Consider:

- Indian skin tones and hair textures in lighting tests
- Local clothing and usage habits
- Urban, small-town or regional context
- Language visible on packaging or signage
- Food preparation and serving conventions
- Accessibility and representation
- Whether imported visual references feel disconnected from the brand

This does not mean every image must contain an obvious Indian visual cue. It means the setting, people and behaviour should feel believable for the audience you serve.

## Plan the Approval Process

A photography project can slow down when several people provide conflicting feedback. Name one primary contact and one final approver in the brief.

Define when you will approve:

- The creative concept
- The mood board
- The shot list
- Location and styling
- Model selection
- A test image, if applicable
- The first edited set
- The final files

Ask the agency how feedback should be submitted. Consolidated comments in one document are easier to act on than separate messages from a founder, marketing manager and designer.

### Create a shot list, but keep room for judgement

A shot list protects essential requirements. It might include:

- Product front, side and back
- Product with packaging
- Product being opened
- Product in use
- Detail texture
- Founder portrait
- Team group
- Workspace wide shot
- Service interaction
- Empty background composition
- Vertical crop
- Horizontal crop

The creative team may recommend additional shots during planning. Allow some flexibility for useful variations, but mark the non-negotiable images clearly.

### Plan a backup

Products may arrive damaged, weather may change, locations may become unavailable and key people may fall ill. Include practical alternatives:

- Indoor location if the outdoor setup is unusable
- Spare product units
- Alternative staff members
- Backup date
- Additional props
- A plan for photographs that do not depend on natural light

A backup plan is particularly important for businesses coordinating with schools, clinics, field programmes or multiple locations.

## A Practical Brand Photography Brief Template

You can copy the following structure into a document and complete it before speaking with an agency.

### Project overview

- Brand and organisation name
- Main contact
- Final approver
- Project name
- Business objective
- Desired launch or usage period

### Audience and message

- Primary audience
- Secondary audience
- Main customer need or concern
- Message the images should communicate
- Desired action

### Brand direction

- Brand personality
- Preferred colours and visual cues
- Existing brand guidelines
- References
- Things to avoid

### Photography scope

- Products to photograph
- People to photograph
- Locations
- Product, lifestyle, team or documentary requirements
- Video or motion requirements
- Required social media formats

### Deliverables

- Expected final image categories
- Approximate quantity
- File types and resolution
- Crops and adaptations
- Retouching level
- Delivery method
- Raw file requirement

### Production information

- Available dates
- Location access
- Working hours
- Product availability
- Models and participants
- Props and styling
- Travel requirements
- Safety or privacy restrictions

### Legal and approval

- Consent requirements
- Usage rights
- Confidentiality
- Portfolio permissions
- Internal approvers
- Feedback process
- GST and invoice details

The agency may revise this template during discovery. That is part of agency planning, not a sign that your original brief was inadequate.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long should a brand photography brief for an agency be?

There is no fixed ideal length. A simple founder portrait session may need only a few pages, while a D2C product shoot with models, multiple locations and social media adaptations may require a more detailed document. Aim for completeness rather than length, and use tables or bullet points where they make information easier to scan.

### What is the difference between a creative brief and a photography brief?

A creative brief usually explains the larger campaign, audience, message, brand tone and communication objective. A photography brief goes further into the visual production: products, people, locations, shot types, formats, styling, deliverables, permissions and logistics. For a small project, both can be combined into one document.

### Should I include competitor photographs in the brief?

You can include competitor references to explain the category, but do not ask an agency to copy them. Use references from different industries to show lighting, composition or mood, and clearly explain what you like and what you want to avoid. Your final direction should be based on your brand and audience.

### Do I need professional models for product photography?

Not always. A founder, staff member or customer may be more credible for some brands, particularly local services, schools, clinics and community organisations. Professional models can be useful when you need consistent availability, specific styling or commercial usage rights, but consent and usage terms should be documented in either case.

### Should the agency provide raw photographs?

This depends on your workflow and the agreement. Raw files are not always ready for direct publication and may require specialised software or consistent editing. If you need them for archival or future work, discuss storage, ownership, file format and any additional fee before the shoot.

### How do I make photographs useful for social media?

Tell the agency about the platforms, placements and content formats before the shoot. Request a mix of portrait, square and landscape compositions where necessary, including some images with negative space for text. Also clarify whether you need only photographs or complete social media designs with copy, branding and captions.

## Where to Start

Begin by writing the business objective, audience, required image categories and intended platforms. Then collect your brand assets, prepare a product and participant list, identify consent requirements, and create a short reference pack showing the desired visual direction.

Send the completed brief to two or three suitable creative agencies and ask each one to respond with scope, deliverables, assumptions, production requirements, usage rights and GST treatment.
